title: Trump Declares Strait of Hormuz Will Become U.S. Territory After Iran War
excerpt: At a rally in New York, the president said he would claim the strategic waterway as American territory once Iran is defeated, despite traffic remaining 90% below pre-war levels and shipping largely avoiding the U.S.-backed route.
body:
• Trump told a rally in Garden City, N.Y. on Friday that he will declare the Strait of Hormuz "a territory of the United States" after the war with Iran ends
  • Ship-tracking data shows traffic through the strait has collapsed to just 14 vessels per day, down from 130+ before the war, with only 2 of 166 August crossings using the U.S.-backed route along Oman
  • Gas prices have risen to a national average above $4 per gallon, up from $2.98 before the U.S.-Israel attack on Iran in February, which Trump said he will "never apologize" for
  • The International Energy Agency says the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed again since June's ceasefire deal collapsed in July

President Donald Trump declared on Friday that he intends to make the Strait of Hormuz a territory of the United States once the war with Iran concludes — his most aggressive claim yet over the strategic waterway through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil once flowed.

"After we finish defeating Iran, I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," Trump told a rally before law enforcement members in Garden City, New York. "We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to."

Rhetoric vs. Reality on the Water

Trump's assertion of control over the strait stands in stark contrast to conditions on the waterway. Ship-tracking data shows just 14 vessels crossed the strait on Tuesday — down from more than 130 daily transits before the war. Traffic averaged only 26 crossings per day in July and 33 in June, according to the Wall Street Journal.

https://x.com/imetatronink/status/2088370488020258868

The data reveals an even more telling detail: of 166 crossings tracked in August, only two used the U.S.-backed route along Oman's coast. About half of ships chose the route administered by Iran, while the rest went dark, switching off their location beacons entirely.

"The southern Omani corridor cannot presently be considered a reliably protected transit route."

— Dimitris Maniatis, CEO of maritime-risk company Marisks

The International Energy Agency said Wednesday that the strait has been effectively closed again since June's ceasefire deal collapsed in early July, when Iran targeted commercial ships and Washington accused Tehran of violating the agreement.

Energy and Economic Fallout

The disruption has driven gas prices to a national average above $4 per gallon, up from $2.98 before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on February 28. Trump acknowledged the spike at Friday's rally but was defiant: "You have to pay a little bit more, you're at $4. I did the right thing. I will never apologize."

Iran's grip on the strait has cost the world more than 2.6 billion barrels of oil since the war began, according to Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser. War-risk insurance for a Hormuz transit has surged to as much as 10% of a ship's value — up from 0.25% before the conflict — potentially adding $3 million to $10 million in insurance costs per voyage for large tankers.

Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that bringing down gas prices is now the "number one goal of the war," a shift from Trump's original stated objectives of preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon and destroying its missile capabilities.

Legal and Diplomatic Questions

International law does not permit any nation to unilaterally claim sovereignty over an international strait. The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is bordered by Iran and Oman. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, all ships have the right of transit passage through international straits.

Trump's declaration follows a pattern of escalating claims over the waterway. On Wednesday, he posted on Truth Social that "The U.S.A. has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!" In July, he briefly imposed a 20% toll on all cargo before reversing course within 24 hours after backlash from Gulf allies.

Broader War Trajectory

The five-month-old conflict shows no signs of resolution. Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have widened the war by attacking ships at the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea, where a strike on the cargo ship Tihamah on Tuesday killed four sailors — the first Houthi-linked shipping deaths since the war began.

Control of the Strait of Hormuz remains the central sticking point in any potential de-escalation, with both the U.S. and Iran claiming authority over shipping routes and neither willing to yield.
image_caption: The Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula that handles roughly a fifth of global oil transit. President Trump declared plans to claim the strait as U.S. territory.
nri_angle: Rising gas prices and global energy disruptions from the Hormuz crisis directly affect Indian-American households and the broader U.S. economy, while India — one of the largest oil importers through the strait — faces supply chain pressures.
